The White-winged tern (Chlidonias leucopterus) is a small migratory marsh tern whose life history is constrained by the brief availability of ephemeral wetlands across its breeding range in Eurasia. During intensive field studies in Ukrainian deltas, females produced exactly two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], with a single clutch laid annually [F_R_i = single clutch laid annually], yielding a modest reproductive output typical of many semi-colonial larids. Under the thermal conditions representative of the active metabolic period for this species (41 °C [T = 41 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate is effectively constrained to these single annual clutches, as the short Arctic summer permits only one successful nesting attempt before water levels recede. Incubation periods measured in captive breeding colonies under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] revealed that pipping occurs after approximately 20.5 days [ab = approximately 20.5 days], a duration consistent with values recorded for congeners such as Chlidonias hybrida. Developing chicks are entirely dependent on their parents during this interval, and the precise timing of hatching is critical for synchronizing peak food demand with insect emergence.

Neonatal body mass has been documented for closely related species, and available comparative data for the black tern (Chlidonias niger) indicate a hatchling wet weight of 7.25 grams [Wwb = 7.25 grams], a value that likely serves as a reasonable proxy for the White-winged tern given their similar egg sizes and incubation durations. Newly emerged chicks are covered in dense down and are semi-precocial, capable of limited movement but reliant on the adults for thermoregulation and provisioning. Female White-winged terns attain a maximum adult body mass of 73 grams [Wwi = 73 grams], placing them at the smaller end of the body size spectrum among marsh terns. This moderate adult mass reflects the energetic demands of a diet composed primarily of aquatic insects, small fish, and crustaceans captured during foraging flights low over the water surface. The disparity between the 7.25 grams [Wwb = 7.25 grams] birth mass and the 73 grams adult female mass underscores the rapid growth trajectory required during the short breeding season, wherein chicks must achieve independence before their natal wetlands dry out in late summer.

Fledging represents a critical developmental milestone in the White-winged tern, as the ability to fly is essential for following adult birds to new foraging patches and for undertaking the autumn migration to sub-Saharan Africa. Field observations indicate that chicks achieve their first sustained flight at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], measured under the typical ambient conditions of the breeding season at 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This rapid development to fledging is remarkably short compared to other tern species of similar body mass, reflecting strong selection pressure imposed by the ephemeral nature of the species nesting habitat. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain in family groups for several additional weeks, during which the adults continue to provide food while the young birds refine their aerial hunting skills. The correlation between the 12 day fledging age and the overall 20.5 day [ab = 20.5 day] incubation period reveals a compressed developmental timetable from egg-laying through fledging that occupies roughly 33 days under optimal conditions.

Mark-recapture data from breeding colonies in southeastern Europe suggest that individuals reach sexual maturity at 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching], determined by the appearance of secondary sexual plumage characteristics and the onset of courtship behaviors at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This age at puberty is measured under the active metabolic temperature regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] that characterizes the summer breeding period. However, despite achieving physiological puberty at 36 days, first reproduction is typically deferred much longer, as young birds must acquire sufficient foraging experience and establish territories before they can successfully breed. The interval between hatching and puberty is carefully timed such that gonadal maturation coincides with the peak abundance of insect prey, which fuels the high energetic costs of egg production and chick-rearing for the subsequent breeding season.

Longevity records for the White-winged tern are primarily derived from banding studies of the closely related black tern (Chlidonias niger), given the logistical challenges of marking sufficient numbers of the less abundant congener. Data from long-term ringing programs in Poland and Hungary indicate that the maximum lifespan recorded for C. niger reaches 21 years [am = 21 years], under the thermal conditions typical for temperate breeding populations at 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. First successful reproduction in these banded individuals was documented at an age of 730 days after birth [tR = 730 days after birth], also recorded at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], revealing a substantial lag between the attainment of puberty at 36 days and the ability to actually secure a nest site and attract a mate. This two-year delay before first breeding likely reflects the intense competition for limited nesting habitat and the time required to achieve full adult plumage. The combination of a long potential lifespan of 21 years and a deferred age at first reproduction of 730 days shapes a life history strategy that emphasizes adult survival and iteroparity over early, risky breeding attempts.
